items.followUp: State four differences between a compound and a mixture.

rubric.why: Elements in a compound combine chemically in a definite proportion.
rubric.description: States that a compound has a fixed composition or definite proportion of elements.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the fixed composition or proportion of elements in a compound.

accept: different from those of its constituent elements
rubric.why: A compound has properties different from those of the elements that form it.
rubric.description: Compares a compound’s properties with those of its constituent elements.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the compound’s properties differ from those of its elements.

rubric.why: The elements of a compound can be separated only by chemical means.
rubric.description: States how the elements in a compound can be separated.
rubric.how: Award for stating that chemical methods or chemical change are needed to separate the elements.

rubric.why: A compound is homogeneous and has characteristic physical constants.
rubric.description: Gives a further property, such as uniform composition or a definite melting or boiling point.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning that a compound is homogeneous, uniform throughout, or has a definite melting or boiling point.

modelAnswer: A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed proportion by mass.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements.
Its elements can be separated only by chemical methods, not by physical methods.
A compound is homogeneous and has a uniform composition throughout.
A pure compound has definite physical constants, such as a definite melting point and boiling point.

items.followUp: Define a compound and give two examples of compounds.

accept: sharing one or more pairs of electrons
rubric.why: A covalent bond forms when atoms share electron pairs.
rubric.description: Defines a covalent bond in terms of sharing electron pairs.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a covalent bond is formed by sharing one or more pairs of electrons.

rubric.why: A single covalent bond consists of one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.description: Describes a single covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award for identifying a single covalent bond as involving one shared pair.

rubric.why: A double covalent bond consists of two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.description: Describes a double covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award for identifying a double covalent bond as involving two shared pairs.

rubric.why: A triple covalent bond consists of three shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.description: Describes a triple covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award for identifying a triple covalent bond as involving three shared pairs.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is a chemical bond formed between atoms by sharing one or more pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond is formed by sharing one pair of electrons; for example, H₂.
A double covalent bond is formed by sharing two pairs of electrons; for example, O₂.
A triple covalent bond is formed by sharing three pairs of electrons; for example, N₂.

items.followUp: Explain the main observations of Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model places positive charge and almost all the atom’s mass in a very small, dense nucleus.
rubric.description: Describes the nucleus as very small, dense and positively charged, with most of the atomic mass concentrated in it.
rubric.how: Award for describing the small, dense, positive nucleus and stating that almost all atomic mass is concentrated there.

rubric.why: Most of an atom’s volume is empty space.
rubric.description: States that most of the atom is empty space.
rubric.how: Award for explicitly stating that most of the atom or its volume is empty space.

rubric.why: The model places electrons revolving around the nucleus.
rubric.description: Describes electrons as revolving or orbiting around the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award for identifying electrons and their motion around the nucleus.

rubric.why: A suitable diagram should show a central nucleus and electrons around it.
rubric.description: Provides a labelled representation of the atom, with the nucleus at the centre and electrons around it.
rubric.how: Award for a diagram or clear textual schematic that identifies the nucleus and electrons and shows their arrangement around the nucleus.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s atomic model has the following features:
An atom has a very small, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre.
Almost all the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus.
Electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular paths; the electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and electrons holds them in the atom.
Most of the volume of an atom is empty space.
Diagram:
e⁻
e⁻ (  [ + nucleus ]  ) e⁻
e⁻
The nucleus is at the centre, electrons are around it, and the space between them is mostly empty.

items.followUp: What is the Tyndall effect? Give one example of a colloid that shows it.

rubric.why: A colloid is heterogeneous, although it may appear uniform to the naked eye.
rubric.description: States the nature of a colloid.
rubric.how: Award for identifying a colloid as heterogeneous.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles remain dispersed and do not settle on standing.
rubric.description: Describes what happens to colloidal particles when left standing.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the particles do not settle or remain dispersed.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles scatter light, producing the Tyndall effect.
rubric.description: Describes the scattering of light by colloidal particles.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning light scattering or the Tyndall effect.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles undergo continuous random motion.
rubric.description: Describes the movement of colloidal particles.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning Brownian movement, Brownian motion or continuous random motion.

modelAnswer: A colloid is a heterogeneous mixture, although it may appear homogeneous to the naked eye.
Its particles remain dispersed and do not settle on standing.
Colloidal particles scatter light, producing the Tyndall effect.
The particles show continuous, random Brownian movement.

items.followUp: Write the electronic configuration of calcium (atomic number 20) in shells.

rubric.why: A neutral magnesium atom has 12 electrons because its atomic number is 12.
rubric.description: Identifies the number of electrons in a neutral magnesium atom.
rubric.how: Award for stating that magnesium has 12 electrons.

rubric.why: Magnesium’s 12 electrons are arranged in shells as 2, 8, 2.
rubric.description: Gives magnesium’s shell electronic configuration.
rubric.how: Award for the correct shell configuration 2, 8, 2.

modelAnswer: Magnesium has atomic number 12, so a neutral magnesium atom has 12 electrons.
Its electronic configuration in shells is 2, 8, 2.
Magnesium has two electrons in its outermost shell.

items.followUp: The distance between the nuclei of two bonded hydrogen atoms is 74 pm. Calculate the atomic radius of hydrogen.

rubric.why: Atomic radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms.
rubric.description: Defines atomic radius using the internuclear distance of identical bonded atoms.
rubric.how: Award for stating that atomic radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms.

rubric.why: Half of the 74 pm internuclear distance in H₂ is 37 pm.
rubric.description: Gives the hydrogen atomic-radius example and its value.
rubric.how: Award for giving 37 pm as the hydrogen atomic radius.

modelAnswer: Atomic radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms bonded together.
For example, the internuclear distance in an H₂ molecule is 74 pm.
Atomic radius of hydrogen = 74 pm ÷ 2 = 37 pm.

items.followUp: What determines an element’s position in the modern periodic table, and why?

rubric.why: Atomic number equals the number of protons and identifies the element.
rubric.description: Links atomic number with the proton number and element identity.
rubric.how: Award for stating that atomic number gives the number of protons or determines the identity of an element.

rubric.why: Atomic number determines electron arrangement and chemical properties; isotopes of an element can have different masses despite having the same atomic number.
rubric.description: Explains why atomic number is more fundamental than atomic mass.
rubric.how: Award for linking atomic number to electronic configuration and chemical properties, or for explaining that isotopes have the same atomic number but different masses.

modelAnswer: The atomic number is more fundamental than atomic mass because it gives the number of protons in an atom and therefore determines the identity of the element.
It also determines the electronic configuration and hence the chemical properties of the element.
Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but different atomic masses.
